title: Female Flower, Bract, Stigma, and Inflorescence Anatomy
objective: Identify female reproductive structures without using the colloquial word “calyx” for every surrounding tissue.

terms.definition: A modified leaf associated with a flower or inflorescence.
The receptive surface on which pollen can hydrate and germinate.
The structure containing the ovule and later contributing to fruit formation.

coreScience: Female cannabis inflorescences are made of many small pistillate flowers associated with bracts and small leaves. Each pistillate flower contains a one-ovule ovary and two elongated stigmatic branches that extend outward. The surrounding bract becomes a prominent resin-bearing tissue and is one of the densest sites of capitate-stalked glandular trichomes.

Cannabis literature and grower language use “bract” and “calyx” inconsistently. This encyclopedia adopts the following controlled convention: calyx means the collective sepal whorl, while the prominent resin-bearing leaf-like structure surrounding the pistillate flower is labeled the bract. That is a declared terminology choice tied to the cited anatomical sources, not a claim that every publication uses the terms identically.

The commercial “bud” is an inflorescence, not a single flower. Its density, branching, bract size, leaf proportion, stigma development, trichome distribution, and maturation pattern vary with genetics and environment. Pollination changes resource allocation toward achene and embryo development.
cultivationRelevance: Sample maturity from defined bract locations rather than whichever visible leaf has the most dramatic trichome color. Sugar-leaf glands and bract glands can mature differently.
When inspecting for disease, open dense inflorescences carefully. Exterior appearance can hide senescent tissue, moisture pockets, insects, or Botrytis injury.

misconceptions: A bud is one flower: It is a compound inflorescence containing many small flowers and bracts.
Every swollen resinous structure is a calyx: The commonly referenced structure is usually the bract.
Orange stigmas alone establish harvest maturity: Stigma color is affected by age, pollination, handling, and environment and is only one observation.
evidenceLimits: Cannabis floral terminology has been used inconsistently in cultivation literature. The encyclopedia uses explicit tissue labels and cites the anatomical convention.
